seo.og_description: What to see, eat and expect at Marrakech's legendary main square, from orange juice at breakfast to food stalls after dark.

name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
hero_subtitle: Marrakech's great open-air stage, from orange juice at breakfast to smoke, drums and grilled meat after dark.

overview.title: A Square That Changes Shape All Day
overview.p1: Ask ten people what Jemaa el-Fnaa is and you'll get ten answers: a market, a stage, a giant outdoor restaurant, the city's living room. They're all right. The square sits at the edge of the medina and has been where Marrakech gathers since the city was founded in the 11th century, which is why UNESCO recognised its storytelling, music and street traditions as intangible cultural heritage.
overview.p2: Go in the morning and it feels almost sleepy: a few orange juice carts, dried fruit sellers, pigeons, a handful of tourists squinting at maps. Go back at sunset and it is a different place. Storytellers pull circles of listeners around them, Gnawa musicians start up, and dozens of food stalls appear out of nowhere, wrapped in charcoal smoke.
overview.p3: Nobody agrees on where the name comes from. One popular reading is "assembly of the dead", a nod to the days when the square hosted public executions, but you'll hear other versions too. The square doesn't seem to mind the mystery, and neither will you once you're standing in it with a glass of orange juice in your hand.

moods.title: What to Do at Jemaa el-Fnaa, Hour by Hour
moods.subtitle: The square has three very different personalities. Ideally you'll see at least two.

1.title: Quiet, Bright and Easy to Photograph
1.desc: Fresh orange juice from the carts, a slow loop of the square, and a look at the dried fruit and nut stalls. It's the best moment for photos without a crowd in the frame, and a good time to get your bearings before the souks.

2.title: Rooftops, Storytellers and Golden Light
2.desc: Around 4 pm the circles start to form: storytellers, Gnawa musicians, acrobats. Climb to a rooftop café (Café de France and Café Glacier are the classic choices), order a mint tea and watch the square fill up as the light turns gold.

3.title: Smoke, Drums and the Food Stalls
3.desc: The numbered food stalls are up, the grills are hot and the whole square hums. Walk the full circuit before you sit down, then pick a busy stall and eat with a stranger's elbow next to yours. That is the point.

food.title: What to Eat at the Food Stalls
food.p1: Each stall has a number, a row of benches and someone whose job is to convince you to sit down. Don't take the first invitation. Stroll the whole circuit, see what is grilling, and choose the stall with the busiest benches.
food.li1: Grilled merguez sausages and lamb skewers, the safe and delicious starting point.
food.li2: Harira, the thick tomato and lentil soup, ideal on a cool evening.
food.li3: Fried fish and calamari with a squeeze of lemon.
food.li4: Snail soup (babbouche) if you're feeling brave, and sheep's head if you're feeling very brave.
food.li5: Fresh orange juice from the carts and a bag of dates or dried figs for the walk home.
food.p2: Most stalls post a price board. Check it before you order, and confirm what is included with your plate so there are no surprises when the bill arrives. If it's your first evening in Marrakech and you'd rather have someone else do the choosing, a guided food tour is an easy way in.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Jemaa el-Fnaa

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: Taxis and most walking routes end at the square, so it's an easy landmark to give a driver. Insist on the meter (compteur) in petit taxis. Cars can't enter the medina alleys, so your riad may ask you to meet a porter at the edge.

2.title: Photos and Performers
2.desc: Musicians, henna artists and snake handlers expect a tip if you photograph them, so ask first and agree on an amount. Many travellers skip acts that use chained monkeys or snakes; you'll find plenty to watch without them.

3.title: Staying Comfortable
3.desc: It gets crowded and loud, so wear your bag in front and keep your phone out of back pockets. If someone grabs your hand to start a henna design, just pull away politely and keep walking. Unofficial guides will offer to lead you somewhere; a firm no, thank you is enough.

q1.question: Is Jemaa el-Fnaa free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. There is no ticket and no gate, the square is open around the clock. Where money does change hands is at the orange juice carts, the food stalls, the rooftop cafés and when you tip a performer.

q2.question: What is the best time to go to Jemaa el-Fnaa?
q2.answer: Late afternoon into the evening. From about 4 pm the storytellers and musicians arrive, and the food stalls start setting up. Come at sunset, stay for dinner. If you just want photos without the crowd, go before 10 am.

q3.question: Is Jemaa el-Fnaa safe at night?
q3.answer: Most visitors have a great time there, and the square is busy until late. Keep your phone and wallet out of easy reach, ignore anyone who grabs your hand to start a henna drawing, and expect a lot of friendly (and slightly pushy) invitations to sit at a stall.

q4.question: How long should I spend at Jemaa el-Fnaa?
q4.answer: Plan on 1.5 to 3 hours. That is enough for a walk around, a juice, a rooftop view and something to eat. If you like people-watching, you will happily stay longer.

q5.question: Is the street food at Jemaa el-Fnaa safe to eat?
q5.answer: Plenty of travellers eat there without a problem. Pick a stall with a queue, choose food that is cooked in front of you, and be careful with raw salads and ice if you have a sensitive stomach. Check the price before you sit down.
